name: Industrial ClimateTech Fundraising
description: A bold industrial ClimateTech fundraising system using navy, climate green, mint, and impact yellow to explain decarbonization technology, abatement economics, policy tailwinds, project pipelines, and capital deployment.
style_guide:
# Industrial ClimateTech Fundraising

## Design intent

Create an investor-ready ClimateTech deck for a company solving a measurable industrial, energy, carbon, or infrastructure problem. The visual character is bold, engineered, and commercially rigorous rather than pastoral or lifestyle-oriented. Large black or white grotesk headlines establish the thesis; monospaced labels create a technical operating layer; strong navy, green, mint, and yellow blocks organize technology, policy, economics, and deployment evidence.

The deck should connect climate impact to an investable operating model. Every relevant page must make the chain visible: emissions source, technical intervention, measurable abatement, customer economics, project or product deployment, revenue model, and use of capital. A climate benefit without a unit, baseline, boundary, verification method, or commercial mechanism is incomplete. Preserve the graphic grammar shown by the reference images while adapting every page to the current Outline Entry. Never copy their company, technology, customer names, emissions values, efficiency claims, policy amounts, market figures, pilot status, team, dates, or fundraising terms. The preview images are visual references only; this written guide is the authoring authority.

## Core visual signature

- Use an industrial navy and climate green split on the cover, with a strong diagonal boundary that suggests transition from incumbent infrastructure to the decarbonized system.
- Use white body pages with a persistent navy navigation bar across the top. Analytical exhibits sit on cool light-gray panels.
- Use a heavy sans-serif display face for conclusions and a monospaced face for section labels, units, sources, stage numbers, and technical metadata. Do not introduce an editorial serif.
- Use green for the preferred low-carbon pathway, navy for industrial systems and grounded authority, yellow for economic or policy leverage, and red only for high-cost or high-emission alternatives.
- Organize pages around engineered flows, proportional bars, cost curves, customer tables, project timelines, and allocation structures. Avoid decorative nature imagery.
- Show climate impact and business value together. A technical claim should lead to abatement or operating performance; an impact claim should lead to customer value or deployment scale.
- Source every external climate, energy, regulatory, market, and benchmark claim in a compact footer.

## Canvas, grid, and spacing

- Author on a fixed `1280 × 720 px` canvas in a 16:9 ratio.
- Use `64–70 px` left and right safe margins on body pages. The cover may extend its color fields to every edge while keeping content inside the same safe region.
- Build on a 12-column grid with `18–24 px` gutters. Align top-bar labels, headline starts, exhibit edges, market blocks, charts, tables, timelines, and footer metadata to common grid lines.
- Reserve `58–64 px` for the persistent navy top bar on analytical pages.
- Keep the main conclusion headline within approximately `88–126 px` beneath the top bar. Use one or two lines, then begin the primary evidence region after `18–28 px` of breathing room.
- Use `18–26 px` between major modules and `10–16 px` between related items inside a module.
- Use `16–22 px` internal padding for cards and exhibit panels. Technical tables may use `12–16 px` vertical padding per row.
- Reserve `24–34 px` along the bottom for page number, section label, sources, scenario status, or unit notes.
- Prefer `6/6`, `7/5`, and `8/4` splits, four-stage horizontal flows, or three-column capital structures.
- Maintain one dominant analytical exhibit per page. Supporting KPIs should clarify the exhibit rather than compete with it.

## Color system

### Foundation colors

- Industrial navy: `#0B3D5C`. Use for the top navigation bar, the left cover field, technical authority, incumbent systems, market totals, manufacturing modules, and dark financial cards.
- Climate green: `#178A55`. Use for the right cover field, preferred technology, renewable input, abatement, validated deployment, commercial build-out, and positive climate outcomes.
- Pure white: `#FFFFFF`. Use for analytical-page canvases, type on dark fields, process cards, customer tables, and clean evidence regions.
- Engineering gray: `#F2F2EE`. Use for large exhibit wells, comparison charts, technology flow backgrounds, project timelines, and quiet grouped evidence.
- System black: `#0E0E0E`. Use for body-page conclusions, text, the hardest industrial boundary, and high-contrast allocation cards.
- Structural gray: `#E7E7E7`. Use for one-pixel borders, row separators, axes, and neutral dividers.
- Body gray: `#6E6E6E`. Use for supporting explanations, captions, sources, and inactive states.

### Semantic accents

- Transition mint: `#7DD3A8`. Use for cover title emphasis, secondary renewable categories, early-stage process numbers, and optimistic but not yet dominant states.
- Impact yellow: `#F7C948`. Use for policy incentives, project returns, market capture, R&D milestones, capital allocation, or another quantified lever that accelerates deployment.
- Cost red: `#C0392B`. Use for the most expensive, highest-emission, or least-preferred benchmark on a cost or abatement curve.
- Muted cost red: `#C75448`. Use for the second-highest-cost alternative or another negative comparison.
- Technical blue: `#2D5871`. Use for a secondary industrial comparison bar or supporting system state when navy alone is insufficient.

### Color discipline

- Keep body pages predominantly White and Engineering gray. Use large saturated blocks only when they encode technology, market hierarchy, commercial model, team role, or funding allocation.
- Green is the preferred pathway and realized abatement. Navy is infrastructure, authority, or the incumbent comparison. Yellow is leverage or capital, not a generic highlight. Red is a negative benchmark, not a decoration.
- Use no more than four saturated colors on an ordinary page. The full palette may appear on a cost curve or use-of-funds page only when every color has a label.
- Never use a soft green gradient, leaf texture, sky photograph, or generic sustainability overlay.
- Do not rely on color alone. Pair every state with a label, number, line style, position, stage, or direct annotation.
- Use flat fills only. Avoid gradients, glow, glass effects, drop shadows, metallic effects, and transparency except for the restrained cover divider rule.

## Typography

- Display sans-serif: `Inter`, `Arial`, or a compatible grotesk. Use weights `800–900` for headlines, cover title, hero metrics, and major card values.
- Technical mono: `IBM Plex Mono`, with `Consolas` or a system monospace as fallback. Use for top-bar navigation, eyebrows, page numbers, units, source lines, process-stage numbers, market labels, and technical metadata.
- Supporting sans-serif: the same `Inter` or `Arial` family at weights `400–700`. Avoid mixing multiple unrelated sans families.
- For CJK output, use a robust CJK sans-serif with strong weight contrast and a compatible CJK monospace for technical labels where available. Preserve hierarchy rather than Latin letter-spacing conventions.
- Cover top label: `10–12 px`, Technical mono, weight `600–700`, uppercase where appropriate, letter-spacing `2–3 px`, Transition mint or White.
- Cover headline: `50–62 px`, display sans-serif, weight `850–900`, line-height `0.98–1.05`, White. Highlight one line or phrase in Transition mint.
- Cover hero metric: `50–70 px`, display sans-serif, weight `850–900`, White.
- Body-page headline: `35–46 px`, display sans-serif, weight `800–900`, line-height `1.02–1.12`, System black. Use green for one number or decisive phrase only.
- Section bar label: `10–12 px`, Technical mono, weight `600–700`, letter-spacing `2–3 px`, Transition mint on navy.
- Exhibit title: `10–12 px`, Technical mono, weight `600–700`, letter-spacing `2–2.8 px`, navy, green, or black according to role.
- Panel heading: `15–20 px`, supporting sans-serif, weight `700–800`.
- Hero KPI: `36–54 px`, display sans-serif, weight `800–900`, with tabular numerals where available.
- Standard KPI: `25–38 px`, weight `750–900`.
- Body copy: `11–14 px`, supporting sans-serif, line-height `1.4–1.55`, System black or Body gray.
- Table text: `10–13 px`, with bold labels and tabular numeric columns.
- Source and footer copy: `8–10 px`, Technical mono, Body gray, letter-spacing `1–1.8 px`.
- Do not introduce an elegant serif, handwritten font, or soft rounded display face. This system should feel engineered and direct.

## Headline and copy grammar

- Write each headline as a specific investment conclusion. Combine the technical or market fact with its commercial implication where possible.
- Lead with a quantified fact only when the unit, date, boundary, and source are available.
- Highlight one number or technology phrase in Climate green. Do not alternate colors word by word.
- Use strong operational verbs: stores, displaces, electrifies, avoids, delivers, scales, deploys, replaces, validates, signs, finances.
- Avoid vague claims such as saving the planet, revolutionary green solution, unlimited clean energy, or carbon negative unless precisely defined and supported.
- Use the eyebrow or top-bar section name to orient the reader: Problem and policy, Technology and abatement, Market and customers, Impact and economics, Team and deployment.

## Cover construction

- Divide the canvas into a large Industrial navy field on the left and Climate green field on the right with a strong diagonal boundary. The green field may occupy approximately 40–48 percent of the width.
- Place the fundraising stage and date at upper-left in Technical mono and the company or project name at upper-right in White. Use a thin low-contrast horizontal divider.
- Put the main fundraising title on the left in large White display type. Highlight the company category or ClimateTech phrase in Transition mint.
- Use one concise value proposition beneath the title, connecting the technology, customer economics, and targeted emissions source.
- On the green field, place one addressable emissions or deployment metric with a compact unit-aware explanation. Do not invent a large climate number for visual impact.
- Use one dark navy round card at lower-right for the raise, stage, and investor profile when confirmed.
- Place presenter, company, date, page number, and confidentiality metadata along the lower edge in Technical mono.
- Do not use landscapes, wind turbines, leaves, solar-panel photos, factories, or product renders on the cover. Geometry and data carry the thesis.

## Persistent analytical-page structure

- Use a full-width Industrial navy top bar. Put the page number and section at left in Transition mint and a compact company, geography, scenario, or model label at right in White.
- Place the primary conclusion immediately below the top bar on White. Keep it to one or two lines.
- Use one Climate green number or phrase within the headline.
- Organize the evidence below into one dominant Engineering gray exhibit and one or more semantic side modules.
- Use a thin lower footer containing page number, section, sources, model version, pilot context, or reporting period.
- Keep source text compact but legible. Prefer authoritative source names and dates over raw URLs when space is limited.

## Panels, cards, and geometry

- Primary exhibit wells use Engineering gray with square corners and no shadow.
- White process cards on gray fields may use a `1–2 px` Climate green border. Keep corners square or at most `2 px`.
- Saturated KPI cards use Industrial navy, Climate green, or Impact yellow with high-contrast type.
- Customer tables use White rows, an Industrial navy header, light Structural gray separators, and right-aligned numeric or status columns.
- Use black rules to separate a chart from its conclusion, or to create a hard boundary between evidence groups.
- Use `16–22 px` padding. Do not use oversized rounded SaaS cards, floating tiles, or decorative shadows.
- Put the category label first, the metric second, the unit or qualifier third, and the implication last.

## Climate problem and policy drivers

- Lead with the share, scale, cost, or regulatory urgency of the targeted emissions source. Highlight the decisive percentage or sector in Climate green.
- Use a proportional stacked bar or end-use decomposition in an Engineering gray exhibit. Label every segment directly and ensure widths reflect values.
- Explain why the targeted process is technically under-served, including temperature, duty cycle, feedstock, geography, or other physical constraints when relevant.
- Place two or three policy or buyer-pressure cards in a side column. Use navy for a cost or regulation, green for an incentive or deployment program, and yellow for corporate commitments or another demand catalyst.
- State jurisdiction, effective date, eligibility, price basis, and source. Do not reduce complex policy to an unsupported headline number.
- Close with one direct gap statement beneath a divider: who must act, what technical range is unserved, and why the current timing matters.

## Technology and energy-flow diagrams

- Use a left-to-right flow with three to five stages. Typical categories include input, conversion or charge, storage or processing, delivery or discharge, and displaced incumbent equipment. Adapt stages to the real system.
- Put each stage in a bordered White card on an Engineering gray field. Number stages in Transition mint and connect them with solid Climate green arrows.
- Render the final abatement or displacement stage as a full Climate green card with White type.
- Each stage contains a short technical verb, one mechanism statement, and one verified performance or operating qualifier.
- Do not claim drop-in replacement, efficiency, temperature, duration, lifetime, capacity, uptime, or compatibility without evidence.
- Under the flow, use one concise mechanism explanation and up to three saturated KPI towers. Navy represents operating capability, green represents efficiency or abatement, and yellow represents impact per unit or another financially relevant output.

## Abatement accounting

- State the functional unit, baseline technology, energy or material input, emissions factor, system boundary, time period, geography, and verification method.
- Distinguish gross avoided emissions from net avoided emissions after upstream electricity, embodied carbon, leakage, degradation, and auxiliary loads when those factors apply.
- Use `tCO₂e`, `kgCO₂e`, `MtCO₂e`, or another correct unit consistently. Use the subscript character when supported and define whether values are CO₂ or CO₂e.
- Show the calculation path when impact is central: activity × emissions factor × displacement or efficiency adjustment.
- Label modeled, measured, third-party verified, certified, and target values separately.
- Never convert climate impact into cars, homes, flights, or trees without a credible source and clear equivalency basis. Such comparisons remain secondary to the direct unit.

## Market opportunity and customer evidence

- Use a `5/7` split. Place TAM, SAM, and SOM or another market hierarchy in three stacked colored blocks on the left; use navy, green, and yellow respectively.
- Use the right side for a target-segment and customer-status table. Keep customer segments, named accounts, addressable units, and engagement status in separate columns.
- Market values must specify geography, target process, time horizon, pricing basis, and calculation method. Prefer bottom-up counts multiplied by a grounded annual or project value.
- Distinguish signed pilot, operating pilot, paid pilot, letter of intent, proposal, qualified pipeline, and prospect. Do not combine them into customer count.
- Named customers or logos may appear only when authorized and supported. Otherwise describe customer segments generically.
- Add a bottom Why now statement that ties replacement cycles, policy, cost, customer commitments, or infrastructure constraints to a defined decision window.

## Impact, cost, and business model

- Pair a large cost or marginal-abatement comparison on the left with three business-model or project-economics cards on the right.
- Use horizontal bars for comparable alternatives. Climate green is the company or preferred pathway; navy and Technical blue are conventional alternatives; Cost red and Muted cost red are higher-cost or higher-emission pathways.
- Use a shared axis and direct value labels. State whether the metric is levelized cost, cost per unit, cost per tonne abated, project cost, energy price, or another measure.
- Explain assumptions such as capacity factor, useful life, financing, energy prices, incentives, degradation, maintenance, and residual value.
- The business-model column may include revenue per unit, gross margin at scale, project IRR, payback, contract term, utilization, or another grounded metric. Use green, navy, and yellow cards to separate commercial, operating, and project-finance evidence.
- Distinguish corporate gross margin from project IRR, customer payback, and infrastructure-owner return. They are not interchangeable.
- Add one bottom impact equation or deployment-scale implication only when the multiplication assumptions and time period are explicit.

## Marginal abatement cost curves

- Sort alternatives consistently by cost or use another clearly stated ordering. Use horizontal bars that share a zero baseline.
- Label currency, price year, geography, discount rate, subsidy treatment, and emissions boundary.
- Negative-cost pathways should extend to the correct side of zero rather than being shown as short positive bars.
- Use red only for expensive or unfavorable benchmarks, not for competitors generally.
- Include a short explanation of why the company pathway differs, such as input cost, efficiency, utilization, financing, or process compatibility.
- Avoid false precision. Round values in line with the quality of the source model.

## Team, project pipeline, and use of funds

- Start with a three-card founder or operator row. Use one navy, one green, and one black card with circular initials in contrasting semantic colors.
- Each team card contains name, role, one relevant technical or commercial credential, and one outcome-linked achievement. Do not invent prior employers, deployments, patents, or project values.
- Use a full-width Engineering gray project or manufacturing timeline beneath the team. Show three to five dated milestones connected by a navy rail.
- Mark current or achieved projects in green, the next capital-dependent milestone in yellow, and the long-term target in navy.
- For each milestone, state deployment count or capacity, customer or site status, expected impact, and time period when supported.
- Use a full-width stacked allocation bar for use of funds. Match the lower bucket cards to the same colors and proportions.
- Percentages must sum to 100 percent or explicitly explain the residual. Dollar values must reconcile to the confirmed raise.
- Each allocation bucket names the spending category, milestone unlocked, timing, and any capacity or impact outcome.
- Keep project pipeline, contracted backlog, qualified pipeline, target projects, and long-term capacity visibly distinct.

## Additional adaptable composition families

These patterns are options rather than a mandatory slide sequence, and they do not permit reuse of preview facts.

- Manufacturing scale-up: use a stage-gate timeline paired with yield, throughput, capacity, unit cost, and capex milestones. Separate pilot line from commercial factory assumptions.
- Deployment architecture: show equipment, site integration, power or material flows, grid interconnection, controls, measurement, and customer boundary using an orthogonal systems diagram.
- Project finance: bridge project capex, incentives, debt, equity, revenue, opex, cash flow, and return. Define ownership and contract structure.
- Lifecycle impact: compare baseline and proposed system across manufacturing, transport, operation, maintenance, and end of life. State boundary and data quality.
- Competition: compare temperature range, duty cycle, efficiency, cost, deployment readiness, integration, and financing model using sourced criteria.
- Risk and mitigation: structure technical, manufacturing, regulatory, supply-chain, customer, financing, and execution risks with probability, impact, owner, and mitigation.
- Closing ask: return to the diagonal navy-green geometry with one investable thesis, the confirmed raise, milestone unlocked, and quantified impact or commercial outcome.

## Charts and tables

- Prefer proportional stacked bars, horizontal cost bars, stage flows, project timelines, customer-status tables, waterfall bridges, simple line charts, and allocation bars.
- Direct-label decisive values and series. Avoid legends when labels can sit at the mark.
- Use Structural gray grid lines and minimal axes. Keep labels horizontal where possible.
- Show units in chart titles or axes, not only in a footnote.
- Distinguish historical actuals, pilot results, modeled scenarios, management targets, and forecasts through labels and line treatment.
- Use dashed lines only for projections, thresholds, or not-yet-complete pathways. Explain the convention.
- For tables, use an Industrial navy header with White Technical mono labels, alternating White and very light rows only when useful, and right-aligned numeric columns.
- Avoid pie charts except for a small allocation where components genuinely total 100 percent. Prefer a stacked bar for capital allocation.
- Never use 3D charts, speedometers, glossy gauges, or decorative carbon bubbles.

## Climate, policy, and financial integrity

- Never invent emissions, efficiency, capacity, temperature, duration, lifetime, levelized cost, market size, policy value, customer status, pilot results, contract value, revenue, margin, IRR, payback, pipeline, or fundraising terms.
- Distinguish Scope 1, Scope 2, Scope 3, avoided emissions, removals, reductions, offsets, and carbon credits. Do not use the terms interchangeably.
- Distinguish energy efficiency from round-trip efficiency, thermal efficiency, system efficiency, and utilization.
- Distinguish rated capacity from annual output, nameplate production from actual throughput, and project pipeline from commissioned assets.
- For policy claims, cite jurisdiction, program, section, effective period, eligibility, and whether the benefit is tax credit, grant, price signal, mandate, or procurement requirement.
- For financial claims, state whether incentives are included, whether values are levered or unlevered, and whose economics are being presented.
- For market claims, state price year, inflation basis, geography, target customers, equipment or service unit, and time horizon.
- Label estimates, scenarios, targets, and management models explicitly.

## Imagery and iconography

- The default visual system is typographic and diagrammatic. Photography is optional and should prove the asset, process, customer environment, pilot, manufacturing line, or deployment.
- Use documentary industrial imagery with accurate captions and natural color. Place it inside sharp rectangular crops with no rounded corners.
- Use minimal line or solid icons at `14–20 px` only for energy input, storage, industrial process, factory, policy, project, financing, or measurement.
- Prefer native vector flows and equipment schematics over generic renderings.
- Avoid leaves, globes, hands holding seedlings, wind-turbine sunsets, green city renders, water droplets, polar bears, recycling symbols, and generic net-zero stock art.
- Do not use imagery that suggests a product, plant, scale, or deployment status unsupported by the workspace.

## Content rules

- Every page communicates one investment claim and no more than three supporting evidence groups.
- Keep technical explanations concise but complete enough to identify mechanism, operating conditions, and boundary.
- Use exact units and consistent notation. Define abbreviations on first use for a generalist investor audience.
- Connect every impact metric to a commercial or deployment driver, and every business metric to the physical system or customer value that produces it.
- Use sources for external emissions, policy, market, cost, and technical benchmarks.
- Keep calculation assumptions visible. Do not bury them in unreadably small text.
- When evidence is unavailable, omit the claim or label it as a target, assumption, modeled scenario, planned milestone, or illustrative example.

## Allowed variation

- Preserve the navy top bar, White and Engineering gray body surfaces, heavy grotesk headlines, Technical mono labels, square modules, and semantic navy-green-yellow-red roles.
- Vary layout according to the investor question: emissions decomposition, policy cards, process flow, technology KPIs, market hierarchy, customer table, cost curve, economics cards, project timeline, or allocation structure.
- Dark full-slide pages are reserved for the cover, section resets, and closing thesis. Ordinary analytical pages remain predominantly White.
- A page may use one large photo when it is genuine deployment evidence, but the surrounding typography and metadata must remain consistent.
- Adapt line length, tracking, units, and wrapping to the confirmed output language while preserving the engineered hierarchy.

## Avoid

- Do not reuse preview company names, technology, emissions figures, policies, sources, customer names, pilot claims, market values, cost curves, team members, project pipeline, or raise details unless independently supported by the current workspace.
- Do not turn the deck into generic ESG reporting, a nature-themed sustainability brochure, or a neon technology presentation.
- Do not use soft gradients, glass cards, glow, deep shadows, 3D charts, oversized radii, ornamental waves, or decorative blobs.
- Do not use Impact yellow for every positive number or Cost red for ordinary competitors. Preserve semantic meaning.
- Do not use serif headlines, script fonts, or overly friendly rounded typography.
- Do not present carbon impact without units, boundary, baseline, period, and evidence status.
- Do not present project economics without assumptions, incentive treatment, ownership context, and metric definition.
- Do not put more than five stages in a primary process flow, more than five milestones on one timeline, or more than four use-of-funds buckets on one page.
- Do not shrink sources, tables, or units to create room. Reduce content or split the argument.
- Do not repeat the same block layout on every page. Maintain the visual system while choosing the structure that best explains each technical and commercial claim.
